overview: **Simulated, balanced profiles:** these 243 lineworker interviews are generated cases, not survey evidence or population estimates.
**Field safety** remains central while thinking AI changes dispatch, routes and records before capable robots reach physical repairs.
**Paid training and real vacancies** matter alongside savings, household bills and affordable retirement when workers consider changing roles.

S0.headline: Most lineworkers keep their shifts and physical checks when AI brings only modest change.

whatTheyDo.text: Bianca Novak plans to keep overhead repair rota and check isolation logs before climbs.
Bianca Novak plans to save one takeaway cost each week from new pay.
Yusuf Okafor plans to check AI handovers against notebook and improve unclear template.
Marco Dubois plans to cancel monthly family cinema outing to cover mortgage costs.
Zoe Moreau plans to bring logged AI summary errors to the monthly crew meeting.

whatTheySay: **Human checks** still confirm isolation, pole numbers and damaged equipment after software drafts a work record.
**Small software gains** can help paperwork without replacing a crew at a physical fault.
whatTheyThink: **Pay and savings** shape household security even when technology changes little.
**Wrong records** remain a practical concern because a tidy summary can mislead the next crew.
howTheyFeel: **Calm** is the most common response while regular field work looks secure.
**Existing bills** still leave some profiles anxious despite the mild technology scenario.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.69 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.00 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
The learn-ai action appears for 2 of 81 resistant profiles, versus 39 of 81 adaptive profiles.

quotes.name: Daria Usman
quotes.text: Last February I sold my old road bike to make rent. I don't want to be doing that every year.

quotes.name: Carlos Young
quotes.text: An AI outage map can point at a street; my line crew still has to find the broken wire.

quotes.name: Wendy Quinn
quotes.text: A quiet year for AI will not make my junior lineworker wage fill an empty savings account.

thoughts.text: My income or household budget still needs careful watching.
My work still depends on contracts, projects, or staffing decisions.
My work or income should stay steady in this small change.
I still need time to learn and qualify in this trade.
Small software gains still need safe field checks and realistic schedules.

S1.headline: Lineworkers test new planning tools while questioning whether faster schedules leave safe time and paid hours.

whatTheyDo.text: Bianca Novak plans to compare three generated route plans against pole clearances on site.
Jade Abbott plans to record dispatch estimates against isolation and repair times.
Jade Abbott plans to bring timing records to the union safety group.
Adam Santos plans to cut weekend trips if linework overtime actually falls.
Fatima Yilmaz plans to pay half of remaining callout premiums toward mortgage if premiums continue.

whatTheySay: **Dispatch changes first**, while crews still need access, correct fittings and time to isolate a line.
**Field feedback** should correct bad routes and targets before crews must depend on them.
whatTheyThink: **Office cuts** may shift checking onto field crews or reduce callouts.
**Crew knowledge** still matters, but some households could lose income even without losing a whole job.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety** is the most common mood as some picture less paid work or tighter household finances.
**Unease** also reflects unsafe targets and apprentices losing practical support while personal wages remain secure.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.74 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.10 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
The learn-ai action appears for 9 of 81 resistant profiles, versus 78 of 81 adaptive profiles.

quotes.name: Sara Ziegler
quotes.text: I like picking up tools early, but I won't sign a crew onto a timetable made by something that can't smell a hot insulator.

quotes.name: Zoe Moreau
quotes.text: I can learn a map system, but I can’t learn back a lost second checker after an accident.

quotes.name: Wendy Quinn
quotes.text: A scheduling screen can move my start time, but it cannot teach me a safe power line repair.

S2.headline: The short AGI warning prompts job searches and training as capable robots could reach line repairs around 2031.

whatTheyDo.text: Bianca Novak plans to apply to nearby line crews if the company posts field cuts.
Carlos Silva plans to take company-funded robot testing training if it leads to a paid roster.
Bianca Novak plans to cancel planned kitchen renovation and cut discretionary spending.
Bianca Novak plans to keep taking line repair shifts while awaiting the company crew plan.
Jade Abbott plans to ask union representatives for paid robot trials and stop-work authority.

whatTheySay: **Thinking AI in 2028** changes planning before capable field robots arrive around 2031.
**Paid trials and stop controls** matter before machines handle real faults.
whatTheyThink: **Lost hours or premiums** could strain bills before a replacement role appears.
**Savings buy time**, while training still needs funding and an actual wage at the end.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety and alarm** dominate when workers picture physical repairs moving to robots.
**A cash buffer** can support a careful response without making an equivalent job certain.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.51 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 3.00 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
The retrain action appears for 40 of 81 early profiles, versus 35 of 81 late profiles.

quotes.name: Sara Ziegler
quotes.text: By 2031 I'd be 32, and a robot that can do the climb could take the premium that paid for my savings, even if a human remains to sign off.

quotes.name: Carlos Young
quotes.text: A robot can recover from a bad test in the yard; a power line crew owns the dark street afterward.

quotes.name: Erik Wagner
quotes.text: Three years until robots is not the same as three years of wages.

S3.headline: Five years of warning makes paid training a common plan, while workers check whether new duties carry real wages.

whatTheyDo.text: Jade Abbott plans to apply for paid inspection training after 2031 if salary covers mortgage.
Bianca Novak plans to keep line repair shifts while trialling supervised inspection tools.
Rafael Garcia plans to apply for trial technician role after 2031 if pay covers mortgage.
Bianca Novak plans to overpay mortgage from postponed car budget while both incomes hold.
Wendy Lopez plans to join trade association meeting on apprentice hours and human stop rules.

whatTheySay: **Field trials** should include bad weather, awkward poles and missed faults before robots arrive around 2034.
**Preparation time** should include paid learning and practical work for apprentices.
whatTheyThink: **New inspection or testing roles** may fit existing skills, but a title is not a job offer.
**Household costs** keep funding, course timing and replacement pay central to a move.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety** remains common even with a longer planning window.
**Extra time** gives some workers room to compare real training and job offers.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.94 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.23 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
The retrain action appears for 62 of 81 early profiles, versus 41 of 81 late profiles.

quotes.name: Wendy Quinn
quotes.text: A retirement date written on paper will not replace the junior lineworker wage in my kitchen.

S4.headline: A decade allows staged career and household planning, with physical repair robots still arriving about three years after thinking AGI.

whatTheyDo.text: Bianca Novak plans to renew linework certificate and check paid inspection openings annually.
Jade Abbott plans to apply for company mentor role after 2036 if pay meets household needs.
Rafael Garcia plans to complete assessor course within two years if paid trainer route exists.
Bianca Novak plans to overpay mortgage modestly while both household wages continue.
Carlos Silva plans to wait for customers and six months savings before funding repair shop.

whatTheySay: **A longer runway** can support practical teaching, field trials and preparation before capable robots arrive around 2039.
**Safety authority** should remain clear when workers check or stop a machine repair.
whatTheyThink: **Future wages** still matter for mortgages, children or retirement budgets.
**Later roles** in inspection, teaching or testing depend on actual duties and pay.
howTheyFeel: **Unease** is the most common response as workers weigh longer-term changes.
**Calm and anxiety** both remain: extra notice does not give every household the same financial room.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.54 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.36 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
The retrain action appears for 61 of 81 early profiles, versus 2 of 81 late profiles.
